passages.text: Car factories have used robots for decades. Most, however, are anchored to the floor and repeat a single motion, such as welding a seam, thousands of times a day. [A] A new generation of humanoid robots, with two arms, two legs, and cameras for eyes, is now being tested on assembly lines in the United States and China. [B] Their appeal lies in their anatomy. Factories were designed for human workers. A machine built like a person can therefore reach the same shelves, climb the same stairs, and use the same tools without the building being redesigned around it. [C] For now, the trials are rudimentary. The robots mostly carry parts from one station to another, and they work far more slowly than people. [D] Even their makers admit that years of testing lie ahead before the machines can handle tasks that demand nuanced judgment.

In August 2024, an electric car parked in the underground garage of a large apartment complex in Incheon caught fire early in the morning. The blaze burned for about eight hours, destroyed or damaged well over a hundred vehicles, and left many households without water or electricity for days. Fires in lithium-ion batteries are notoriously hard to extinguish because of a process called thermal runaway. Once one cell overheats, it sets off its neighbors. The battery then keeps generating its own heat even when it is doused with water. In an enclosed garage, smoke and heat accumulate rapidly, making it dangerous for firefighters to get close. After the fire, some apartment complexes moved to prohibit electric cars from their underground garages, and the government pressed carmakers to disclose who made their batteries.

In the late twentieth century the Japanese astrophysicist Koryo Miura devised a way of folding a flat sheet that has since found applications far beyond paper. In a Miura fold, the sheet is creased into a grid of slightly slanted parallelograms. The result can be collapsed into a compact block and then opened again in one smooth motion just by tugging on two opposite corners. Because all the folds move together, the sheet unfolds without tangling or tearing. The technique was tested on a solar panel array carried by a Japanese satellite launched in 1995. Engineers still study it as a way of deploying large structures in space. Back on Earth, some folding maps use the same pattern.

In a well-known 1999 study, the psychologists Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh paired volunteers with a researcher posing as another participant. The researcher deliberately rubbed her face during some sessions and jiggled her foot during others. Without realizing it, the volunteers tended to imitate whichever habit their partner displayed. In a follow-up experiment, the researcher subtly mirrored the volunteers' own postures and gestures. Afterward, those who had been mimicked rated the conversation as smoother and the researcher as more likable than those who had not, although almost none had noticed the copying. The researchers dubbed this unconscious imitation the chameleon effect.

Desert ants of the genus Cataglyphis forage across flat, featureless sand, sometimes wandering more than a hundred meters from their nest in search of food. Once they find something, they run straight home rather than retracing their meandering route. How do they know how far to go? In a 2006 experiment, researchers glued tiny stilts made of pig bristles onto the legs of some ants, elongating their stride, and trimmed the legs of others. The ants on stilts overshot their nest, while those with shortened legs stopped short of it. The results suggest that the ants ____.

Few words sound as lighthearted as bedlam, which today describes nothing worse than a noisy classroom or a crowded sale. Yet the term has a grim origin. It is a shortened form of Bethlem, the name of a London hospital that by the early fifteenth century was housing the mentally ill. For centuries its patients were often kept in chains, and curious members of the public came to stare at them. By the seventeenth century, the word had come to mean any scene of wild confusion. Today, when a parent calls a birthday party bedlam, few listeners picture chained patients. Over the years, the word has <u>lost its edge</u>, keeping its sense of uproar while shedding its link to suffering.

Economics textbooks long used the lighthouse as the classic example of a public good. A lighthouse's beam guides every passing ship, the reasoning went, but its owner cannot make a ship pay for the light it uses. Private firms would therefore never build one, and only governments can. In 1974, however, the economist Ronald Coase examined the history of British lighthouses and found that many had been built and run by private individuals. With official permission, they collected fees from ships when they arrived in port. Coase's point was not that governments are unnecessary, but that economists should study how institutions actually work before pronouncing on what markets cannot do.

The Soviet psychologist Lev Vygotsky maintained that a child's ability should not be judged only by what the child can do alone. Between the tasks a learner can already manage independently and the tasks that are still beyond their grasp lies a middle territory, which he called the zone of proximal development. In this zone, a learner can succeed with help from a teacher or a more capable classmate, for example through a hint, a question, or a demonstration. Work that is too easy teaches nothing new, while work that is far too hard leaves students discouraged. Vygotsky therefore believed that teaching is most effective when it targets this zone.

In 2000 the United States declared that measles was no longer spreading continuously within its borders, a triumph attributed to widespread vaccination. Early in 2025, however, an outbreak that began in a rural community in West Texas swelled into one of the largest the country had seen in decades. Two unvaccinated school-age children died. Measles is among the most contagious diseases known: an infected person can transmit it to most of the unprotected people nearby. Two doses of the vaccine are about 97 percent effective, but to keep the virus from circulating, roughly 95 percent of a community must be immune. Where vaccination rates slip below that threshold, even a single imported case can ____.

In March 2025, the road surface in a busy district of eastern Seoul suddenly gave way. The hole was roughly twenty meters wide, and a motorcyclist who fell into it was killed. The accident rekindled public anxiety about sinkholes, which in cities are usually caused not by natural caves but by what lies beneath the streets. When old water and sewer pipes crack, leaking water can gradually wash away the soil under the pavement. A cavity forms and grows <u>imperceptibly</u> until the road above can no longer bear the weight of traffic. Large construction projects that pump out groundwater can aggravate the problem. Ground-penetrating radar can detect many cavities before they collapse, but surveying every street regularly is prohibitively expensive, so cities must decide which areas to examine first.

(A) In the early 1850s an American mechanic named Elisha Otis devised a remedy. He fitted a hoist with a spring-loaded catch that would grip toothed rails on either side of the shaft if the rope ever broke. In 1854, at an exhibition in New York, he rode an open platform high above a skeptical crowd and ordered the rope to be cut. The platform dropped only a few inches before the catch held it fast.
(B) Within a few decades, passenger elevators with similar safety brakes were being installed in offices and hotels, and architects were free to build far higher than before. Elevators also inverted an old pattern of city life. The top floors, once left to servants and the poor, became the most prestigious addresses in a building, a status that penthouse apartments still enjoy today.
(C) In the early nineteenth century, few buildings rose above five or six stories. Hoists for lifting goods already existed, but they hung from a single rope, and if it snapped, the platform and anything on it plunged to the bottom. Few people were willing to ride in such a machine. Climbing many flights of stairs was grueling, so upper floors were the least desirable part of any building.

Building a house typically takes months and requires dozens of skilled laborers. [A] A growing number of companies now hope to reduce both time and labor by printing homes. A giant robotic arm or gantry moves back and forth over the site, squeezing out a thick paste of concrete layer by layer, much as a desktop printer builds a small plastic toy. [B] In Texas, one builder has used the method to construct an entire neighborhood of roughly one hundred houses. [C] Proponents say that printing generates less waste, since the machine deposits material only where it is needed. [D] Roofs, windows, wiring, and plumbing must still be installed by hand, so printing accelerates only part of the job, and building codes in many places were not drafted with printed walls in mind.

For decades, weather forecasts have been produced by supercomputers that solve equations describing how air, heat, and moisture circulate through the atmosphere. Running these physics-based models consumes hours of computing time. Since 2023, however, several technology companies and research centers have released forecasting systems built on machine learning. Instead of solving the equations directly, these systems extract patterns from decades of archived weather data and can generate a ten-day global forecast in about a minute. In 2025 the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts began running such a model alongside its traditional one. Meteorologists caution, though, that AI models are only as reliable as the historical record they were trained on and may falter in extreme events unlike anything in that record.

Most countries use a system of paper sizes in which a sheet of A4 is precisely half the size of A3, which is in turn half of A2. The trick lies in the ratio of the sides. Every sheet in the series has sides in the proportion of one to the square root of two, roughly 1 to 1.41. Because of this, cutting a sheet in half yields two smaller sheets with exactly the same proportions as the original. The largest standard size, A0, has an area of one square meter. The idea was proposed by a German scientist in the eighteenth century, but it was not widely adopted until the twentieth. The United States and Canada still predominantly use letter-size paper, which lacks this convenient property.

Negotiators often walk into a meeting assuming that whatever one side gains, the other must lose. Researchers call this the fixed-pie bias. A familiar parable illustrates its cost. Two sisters quarrel over a single orange and finally agree to cut it in half. One squeezes her half for juice and discards the peel, while the other grates the peel of her half for a cake and throws away the fruit. Had they simply asked each other why they wanted the orange, each could have received everything she needed. Studies of negotiation suggest that people who disclose their underlying priorities routinely reach better agreements than those who quarrel only over positions.

A solid steel bolt dropped into a harbor sinks instantly, yet a ship made of thousands of tons of steel floats. The explanation goes back to a principle articulated by Archimedes more than two thousand years ago: an object immersed in water is pushed upward by a force equal to the weight of the water it displaces. A steel bolt displaces water weighing far less than the bolt itself. A ship's hull, by contrast, is shaped into a wide, hollow shell filled mostly with air, so it pushes aside an enormous volume of water. What keeps a ship afloat, then, is not the material it is made of but ____.

In 1969 the educator Laurence J. Peter proposed a sardonic rule about organizations. Employees who perform well, he observed, are usually rewarded with promotion to a higher position. If they excel there, they are promoted again. The process halts only when they reach a job they cannot do well, where they then remain. Over time, Peter argued, every position tends to be occupied by someone <u>who has risen to a level of incompetence</u>. The principle was intended partly as satire, but some later studies of sales staff promoted to management have found evidence for it: the best salespeople did not necessarily make the best managers.

Before modern banknotes, many coins contained precious metal, and their value depended on how much gold or silver they held. When a government issued new coins with less silver but decreed them worth the same as the old ones, people behaved predictably. They spent the new, debased coins and hoarded the old, purer ones or melted them down. Soon only the inferior coins were circulating. This tendency is known as Gresham's law, after a sixteenth-century English financier, and it is often summed up as bad money drives out good. Economists note that the same logic can surface wherever two things are officially treated as equivalent but are not equal in reality.

The full moon looks enormous when it rises just above the horizon and noticeably smaller a few hours later, high in the sky. Yet photographs show that its apparent size barely changes. The moon illusion, as it is called, has puzzled thinkers since ancient times, and there is still no single agreed explanation. One popular theory holds that the brain judges the moon near the horizon to be more distant, because it appears beyond faraway trees and buildings, and therefore inflates its size. Whatever the cause, the illusion is a reminder that what we see is not a simple recording of the world but an interpretation constructed by the brain.

In January 2022, South Korea's Serious Accidents Punishment Act took effect after years of public outrage over deaths at construction sites and factories. Earlier laws had mostly penalized site managers and safety officers. The new law, by contrast, can hold business owners and chief executives criminally liable if a worker is killed and the company is found to have neglected its duty to maintain proper safety systems. Penalties can include prison terms. Initially, the law applied only to businesses with fifty or more workers, but in January 2024 it was extended to smaller firms with five or more. Business groups contend that the rules are vague and onerous for small companies, while labor groups reply that the law's real purpose is to make safety ____ rather than an afterthought.

Visitors to Hong Kong are often startled to see skyscrapers under construction wrapped in bamboo. For generations, teams of <u>dexterous</u> workers have lashed bamboo poles together with nylon ties to build scaffolding dozens of stories high. The material is cheap, light, and flexible, and a skilled crew can erect or dismantle it far faster than a comparable metal frame. Bamboo, however, varies in strength from pole to pole, is flammable, and deteriorates in the humid climate, and accidents involving scaffolding have long worried safety officials. In 2025 the city's government announced that metal scaffolding should gradually replace bamboo on many public works projects. Champions of the old craft fear that a distinctive tradition, along with the livelihoods of thousands of scaffolders, may slowly vanish.

(A) That afternoon I made another bracket, and then another. The fourth one matched the drawing to within a hair. He did not praise it; he simply handed me a more intricate drawing. Years later, when I began training apprentices of my own, I kept a scrap bin beside my bench, and on each newcomer's first day I recounted the story of the foreman's notebook.
(B) On my first day at the machine shop, the foreman handed me a steel block, a file, and a drawing of a simple bracket. "Make this," he said, and walked away. I spent the whole morning filing, measuring, and filing again. By lunchtime my hands ached, and the bracket was still a millimeter too thick on one side. When I finally showed it to him, he held it up to the light, nodded once, and tossed it into a bin full of scrap.
(C) I was too stunned to speak. Noticing my dismay, he pulled a battered notebook from his pocket and opened it to a page crowded with pencil sketches. "My first bracket went into that same bin," he said. "So did the next three. Nobody here remembers my first bracket. They remember that I learned to measure twice before I cut."

Cement and steel plants are among the most intractable sources of greenhouse gases. [A] Even if they ran entirely on renewable electricity, making cement would still release carbon dioxide, because the chemical reaction that converts limestone into clinker emits the gas directly. [B] One proposed remedy is carbon capture. Chemical solvents absorb carbon dioxide from a plant's exhaust before it escapes into the atmosphere. The gas is then compressed and transported for permanent storage deep underground. [C] In 2025 a cement plant in Brevik, Norway, began capturing part of its emissions and shipping them to be stored beneath the North Sea. [D] Yet the equipment is expensive, consumes a substantial amount of energy, and typically captures only a portion of a plant's emissions. Critics therefore warn that it must not become a pretext for delaying other cuts.

In the early hours of March 26, 2024, a large container ship leaving the port of Baltimore lost electrical power and drifted into a support pier of the Francis Scott Key Bridge. Within seconds, much of the 2.6-kilometer bridge collapsed into the river. Six members of a road maintenance crew working on the bridge were killed. The toll could have been far higher. Moments before the impact, the ship's crew sent a distress call, and police halted traffic onto the bridge. The disaster prompted engineers to scrutinize older bridges, many of which were designed decades ago, when cargo vessels were far smaller, and to ask whether their piers are adequately shielded against collisions.

In 1965 Stephanie Kwolek, a chemist at the DuPont company, was searching for a lightweight fiber that could reinforce car tires. One of her experimental solutions turned out cloudy and thin, unlike the thick, clear liquids that usually yielded useful fibers. The technician in charge of the spinning machine was reluctant to test it. Kwolek persuaded him to spin it anyway. The resulting fiber proved, weight for weight, about five times stronger than steel. Marketed as Kevlar from the 1970s, it is now used in bulletproof vests, helmets, ropes, and protective gloves. Her story is often cited as evidence that a disappointing result can merit a second look.

In studies conducted in the 1940s and again in the 1970s, psychologists showed chess positions to players of varying skill for just a few seconds. They then asked the players to reconstruct the boards from memory. Masters reproduced positions from real games with astonishing accuracy, placing most pieces correctly, while beginners recalled only a handful. When the pieces were scattered at random, however, the masters' advantage almost vanished. The researchers concluded that experts do not possess extraordinary memories in general. Rather, years of play have stored thousands of familiar configurations in their minds, allowing them to perceive a board as a few meaningful chunks instead of two dozen separate pieces.

Some species of bamboo behave in a way that has long baffled botanists. For decades, sometimes for more than a century, the plants grow and spread without producing a single flower. Then, across an entire region, every plant of the species blooms at almost the same moment, sets seed, and dies. One explanation is that this synchronized flowering ____. The sudden flood of seeds is far more than rats, birds, and other seed-eaters can consume, so enough survive to sprout. Such mass flowering can, however, spark explosions in rat populations, which then devastate nearby crops.

The Greek philosopher Heraclitus, who lived around 500 BCE, left behind only scattered fragments, many of them obscure. The most famous is usually paraphrased as follows: <u>no one ever steps into the same river twice</u>. The water that touched a swimmer's feet yesterday has long since flowed out to sea, and the swimmer, too, has aged and changed in countless small ways. For Heraclitus, the river was a symbol of the whole universe, in which everything is in constant change and stability is merely an appearance. Later thinkers, including Plato, found the idea unsettling, since it seemed to cast doubt on the possibility of lasting knowledge.

On March 27, 1977, two jumbo jets collided on a fog-covered runway on the island of Tenerife, killing 583 people in the deadliest accident in aviation history. Investigators found that misunderstandings in radio communication had played a central role. One crew believed it had been cleared for takeoff when it had not. In addition, an ambiguous phrase from the cockpit was misinterpreted by the control tower. In the decades that followed, aviation authorities standardized the wording pilots and controllers use, and the International Civil Aviation Organization later required those on international routes to demonstrate proficiency in English. The goal was not eloquence but clarity, leaving as little room as possible for a fatal misunderstanding. In this sense, a single foggy afternoon reshaped the language of the skies.

When words migrate from one language to another, they rarely arrive unchanged. Korean, for example, has adopted the English word fighting as a cheer of encouragement, a sense it does not carry in English. Korean speakers also say hand phone for what Americans call a cell phone. Japanese has turned the English word mansion into a term for an ordinary apartment building. Such shifts are not blunders but adaptations. A borrowed word is reshaped to fill a gap in its new language, and it soon belongs to the borrowers rather than to the lenders. Linguists therefore treat loanwords as genuinely new words, with histories of their own.

A digital twin is a virtual replica of a physical object or system, continuously updated with data from sensors on its real-world counterpart. Engineers first applied the idea to complex machines such as jet engines, whose twins can flag signs of wear before a component fails. The concept has since expanded to entire factories and even cities. Singapore, for instance, has built a detailed three-dimensional model of the whole city-state that planners use to simulate how a new building might alter wind flow or sunlight in the surrounding streets. A twin is only as accurate as the data feeding it, and keeping that data current can be a daunting task. Still, the appeal is obvious: testing a change on a digital copy is far cheaper and safer than ____.

Since the Concorde was retired in 2003, no passenger airliner has flown faster than sound. In January 2025, a small experimental jet built by the American startup Boom Supersonic broke the sound barrier over the California desert. The company hailed it as the first time an independently developed jet had done so. The firm hopes the test will pave the way for a larger airliner. Formidable obstacles remain, however. Supersonic flight burns far more fuel per passenger than ordinary flight, and the sonic booms it generates led many countries, including the United States, to <u>prohibit</u> such flights over land decades ago. Engineers are now exploring aircraft shapes that could soften the boom to a muffled thump.

(A) In 1869 the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev published a table that arranged the elements by atomic weight while grouping those with similar behavior in the same column. What set his work apart was its boldness. Where no known element fit, he left a gap, insisting that an undiscovered element belonged there, and he went further, predicting the weight, density, and chemical properties of the missing substances. Few chemists of the day would have risked their reputations on such specific claims.
(B) By the 1860s chemists had identified about sixty elements, but no one had found a convincing way to organize them. Several scientists noticed that elements with similar properties seemed to recur at regular intervals when they were listed in order of atomic weight. Yet their schemes contained awkward exceptions, and their colleagues largely ignored or even ridiculed them. One English chemist who likened the pattern to the octaves of a musical scale was openly mocked at a scientific meeting.
(C) Within two decades, three of the missing elements, now called gallium, scandium, and germanium, were discovered, and their properties closely matched his forecasts. These vindicated predictions won over skeptical chemists. The periodic table, which now hangs on the wall of nearly every science classroom, became the organizing framework of modern chemistry. It was later expanded to accommodate elements that Mendeleev himself never imagined.

adamant 는 '단호한, 꿈쩍도 않는'이라 resolute(굳게 결심한)와 가까워요. 몇 주 동안 불평이 이어져도 버스 차로를 그대로 둔다고 했다는 문맥이 단서예요. apprehensive(걱정하는)·complacent(안주하는)·astute(기민한)는 문장에 넣으면 말은 되지만 '물러서지 않는다'는 뜻이 아니에요.

Choose the option closest in meaning to the underlined part.
The link between the popular diet and a longer life is <u>tenuous</u> at best, resting on a single small survey of volunteers.
tenuous 는 '(근거·관계가) 빈약한, 약한'이라 fragile(무너지기 쉬운)과 가까워요. 자원자 몇 명을 조사한 작은 설문 하나에 기대고 있다는 뒤 내용이 단서예요. controversial(논란이 많은)·conspicuous(눈에 띄는)는 연관성을 꾸밀 수는 있어도 '약하다'는 뜻이 없고, versatile(다재다능한)은 상관없어요.

Choose the option closest in meaning to the underlined part.
Shareholders criticized the board for its <u>lavish</u> spending on a three-day retreat at a luxury resort while factory wages remained frozen.
lavish 는 '(돈을) 아낌없이 쓰는, 호화로운'이라 extravagant(사치스러운)와 가까워요. 공장 임금은 묶어 두고 고급 휴양지 행사에 돈을 썼다는 대비가 단서예요. intricate(복잡한)·secretive(비밀스러운)·impulsive(충동적인)도 spending 을 꾸밀 수는 있지만 '호화롭게 많이 쓴'이라는 뜻은 아니에요.

Choose the option closest in meaning to the underlined part.
Some apps let users <u>circumvent</u> regional restrictions on video services by routing their traffic through servers in other countries.
circumvent 는 '(규제·장애를) 피해 가다'라 dodge(교묘히 피하다)와 가까워요. 다른 나라 서버를 거쳐 지역 제한을 비켜 간다는 문맥이에요. detect(알아내다)·disclose(밝히다)·highlight(강조하다)는 restrictions 와 어울려도 '피해 간다'는 뜻이 아니에요.

Choose the option closest in meaning to the underlined part.
Because of the heavy snowfall, the city council decided to <u>put off</u> its vote on the stadium plan until the following month.
put off 는 '미루다, 연기하다'라 defer 와 같아요. 투표를 다음 달까지 미뤘다는 until 이 단서예요. remove(벗다, 치우다)는 put off 를 글자 그대로 읽은 뜻이고, approve(승인하다)·rescind(철회하다)는 투표를 미루는 것과 달라요.

Choose the word that best fills in the blank.
Heavy fines alone are a surprisingly weak ____ against speeding; drivers slow down far more reliably when they believe they are likely to be caught.
against speeding(과속을 막는) 앞에 오려면 '억제책(deterrent)'이어야 해요. 벌금보다 단속될 거라는 믿음이 더 잘 막는다는 뒤 내용과도 맞아요. merit(장점)·anomaly(예외)·catalyst(촉매)는 against 와 어울리지 않아요.

Choose the word that best fills in the blank.
As young people left for jobs in the cities, the village's population continued to ____, and its last elementary school closed in 2019.
젊은 사람들이 떠나고 마지막 학교가 문을 닫았으니 인구가 '줄어들었다(decline)'가 맞아요. diversify(다양해지다)·accumulate(쌓이다)는 인구를 말할 수는 있어도 학교가 닫은 까닭이 되지 않고, rebound(되살아나다)는 반대예요.

Choose the word that best fills in the blank.
Bright orange vests make road workers ____ to approaching drivers, even in thick fog or at dusk.
밝은 주황색 조끼는 안개나 해 질 녘에도 운전자 눈에 '잘 띄게(conspicuous)' 해 줘요. oblivious(알아차리지 못하는)는 일꾼이 운전자를 못 본다는 뜻이 되어 조끼의 목적과 반대예요.

빈칸부터 alloy 까지가 문장 전체의 주어이고 동사는 was 예요. '~한 것'이라는 명사절을 이끌면서 절 안에서 주어 구실까지 하는 말은 관계대명사 What 뿐이에요. That·Which 는 앞에 선행사가 없어 쓸 수 없고, It 을 넣으면 동사가 둘이 돼요.

When ____ to direct sunlight for several summers, the plastic used in inexpensive garden chairs gradually becomes brittle and loses its color.
주절의 주어 the plastic 이 햇빛에 '노출되는' 쪽이라 수동의 과거분사가 필요해요. When exposed 는 When it is exposed 에서 주어와 be동사를 뺀 분사구문이에요. exposing·having exposed 는 능동이고, it exposes 도 능동이라 뜻이 맞지 않아요.
